t19: Backgammon, with its history spanning over 5,000 years, is one of the oldest board games in the world. In this guide, we've prepared for anyone who wants to learn this game from scratch, combining chance and strategy between two players—from the board to the rules, from strategy to backgammon variants, you'll find everything here.

t24: Backgammon is a dice and strategy game played between two people. Each player has 15 pieces; the goal is to move these pieces in a certain direction on the board, bring them to your home board, and remove them by bearing off. The player who bears off all their pieces first wins the game.
t25: The game involves both chance (dice) and skill (choosing moves). In the short term, dice results can be decisive, but in the long term, the player making the right decisions always comes out ahead.

t56: Each player's sole objective is to bear off all 15 pieces before their opponent. To do this, you must complete three stages:
t58: Move your pieces toward your home board according to the dice results.

t64: To determine who goes first, each player rolls one die. The player rolling the higher number starts. If tied, the dice are rolled again. The starting player makes their first move using the numbers shown on both dice (their own die and their opponent's die). From subsequent turns onward, each player rolls both dice at once.
t66: Players alternate rolling two dice. The numbers shown on the dice are used separately. For example, if you roll a 3 and a 5, you can move one piece 3 points and another piece 5 points; or you can move the same piece 3 points first and then 5 points (or 5 then 3) for a total of 8 points.

t102: Bringing Pieces to Your Home Board
t103: To bear off your pieces, all 15 of your pieces must be in your home board (points 1-6). If you have even one piece on the bar or outside your home board, you cannot start bearing off.
t104: During the process of getting home, interaction with your opponent's pieces continues. If your piece is hit, bearing off stops; you must remove the hit piece from the bar and get it back home again.

t128: The doubling cube, used in tournaments and serious matches, is used to increase the stakes of the game. The cube has the numbers 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64 on its faces; the initial stake is 1.
t132: you can offer doubles to your opponent. This means doubling the stakes.
t133: If your opponent accepts, the stake doubles and the doubling cube now passes to your opponent's side. Only they can offer the next double.
t134: If your opponent refuses, they lose the game at the current stake value (meaning 1 point before the offer).
t135: The doubling cube greatly increases the strategic depth of the game. When your position is strong, offering doubles puts your opponent in a difficult decision: do they continue and take double the risk, or accept the current loss and move on to a new game?
t137: Standard backgammon (also known as long backgammon) is the most common version, but different variations are also played:
t139: In this version played in some regions, pieces move in one direction, and instead of opposite home boards, pieces are borne off from the same side. Rules vary from region to region.
t141: A variant played in Turkish backgammon tradition. Both players move their pieces in the same direction (counterclockwise). There is no hitting; instead, both your pieces and your opponent's pieces can be on the same point, and the opponent's piece is "locked," meaning it cannot move.
t143: Narde, common in the Middle East and Central Asia, is similar to Gul Bara: pieces move in the same direction and there is no hitting.
t145: A variant that originated in the U.S. Navy. Special rules come into play when 1-2 is rolled.
t147: If you're new to backgammon, the following tips will immediately raise your winning percentage:
t149: Whenever possible, keep at least two pieces on each point. Leaving a single piece is a hitting risk.
t151: Especially closing consecutive points in your home board makes it harder for your opponent's bar piece to re-enter.
t153: Known as the "golden point," this is the single most valuable point in backgammon. Closing it early provides a major advantage.
t154: Don't spread pieces too thin, but don't pile them up either:
t155: Having 6-7 pieces on a single point is wasteful; distributing them across several points gives you more options.
t156: When ahead, run; when behind, look for contact:
t157: If you're ahead in the race, reduce contact and bear off quickly. If you're behind, look for opportunities to block your opponent and hit.
t159: There are 36 possible outcomes with two dice. Knowing which distances are likely to be hit helps strengthen your risk calculation.

t173: How many pieces are in backgammon?
t174: Each player has 15 pieces, for a total of 30 pieces. The pieces are in two different colors.
t176: Each player rolls one die; the player rolling higher starts and makes their first move using the two separate dice numbers shown, not the sum of the two dice.
t177: How many moves when rolling doubles?
t178: When you roll doubles, the number shown is played four times. For example, if you roll 3-3, you make four separate moves of 3 points each.
